name: Rosa Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the roofing and carpentry crew at Lund Brothers, a builder in a small market town. We do barns, farm sheds, house roofs and the odd church, out in the villages around us. This week it's re-roofing an old grain barn for a farmer called Haldor, which means pulling off rotten rafters and putting in new oak. I'm out of the house at half six, my husband Erik is a bricklayer at the same firm, so we drive in together and drop the kids at my mother's on the way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You and your husband work for the same firm. What's that like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly good. We know each other's days, we share the van, and Old Man Lund trusts us both. The downside is if Lund has a bad year, we both have a bad year, and we've had a couple of those. I learned roofing from my father, he was at Lund's for thirty years, so it's family in more ways than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could have told them that. I've never used any of it and nobody out here needed it. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked, and at the builders' merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as it is, and that suits me. A barn roof is a barn roof. No program was ever going to climb up there in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Finish Haldor's barn, then the chapel roof at Nordby in the spring, keep paying the mortgage, keep the kids in their clubs. Nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone at Lund's tried to bring in AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lund's grandson set up something on the computer to answer the phone, and it booked a farmer in for a roof on Christmas Day. Old Man Lund turned it off the next morning. That was the end of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna's thirteen and she'd roll her eyes, she thinks I'm a dinosaur. I'd tell her the dinosaur still has a job. Peter would want to know if he can still watch videos, which is all he cares about.

S0.say: I could have told them that: I've never used any of it and nobody out here needed it. I'd say so after church and at the builders' merchant.
S0.think: It means my life stays as it is, and that suits me. A barn roof is a barn roof, and no program was going to climb up there in the wind.
S0.do: Finishes the barn re-roof, then does the chapel roof at Nordby in the spring. Keeps paying the mortgage and keeps the children in their clubs.
S0.quote: It booked a farmer in for a roof on Christmas Day.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa treats AI as something from outside her world, and a phone-answering mishap at the firm confirmed her view. Her identity is tied to her father's trade and a family firm. She speaks with dry humour about being called a dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the cities and offices that'll change, not us. Farmers will still need roofs, and they'll still want someone they know to fix them. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep half an eye on it. If the big firms in the city get machines that put up sheds cheap, they might start coming out to the villages and undercutting Lund's. That's the bit I'd watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Keep working, keep my head down. I wouldn't do any courses, I'm not interested. I'd let it settle and see what it really means before I spent a penny or a Saturday on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a bit stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the city firms might undercut Lund's. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years ago a firm from the city did cheap steel sheds for half the farms round here. Five years later the farmers were ringing Lund's to fix the leaks. People out here remember who turned up when the roof blew off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it cut the paperwork for the farm grants, the farmers would have more money for roofs. So, maybe that. But I'm not holding my breath.

S1.say: It's the cities and offices that'll change, not us. Farmers will still need roofs and will still want someone they know to fix them.
S1.think: I'd keep half an eye on it, because city firms with machines might come out to the villages and undercut Lund's. That's the part I'd watch.
S1.do: Keeps working and refuses any courses. Waits for things to settle before spending money or time on any change.
S1.quote: People out here remember who turned up when the roof blew off.
S1.fieldNote: Her confidence rests on local loyalty and memory of cheap outsiders failing. She sees the threat as city firms rather than machines themselves. She's not hostile, just unwilling to move until she must.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and the people who built it never held a hammer in their lives. I'd say they've no idea what they're doing to towns like ours. I'd say it loud at the builders' merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be terrified. Erik and I both work at Lund's, and if Lund can buy a robot that does roofs and walls, he doesn't need either of us. We've got about two months of money saved, a mortgage, two kids, and in two years I'm not going to become a computer person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, Anna's riding lessons, Peter's football trip, the car we were going to replace. I'd go to the pastor and to my mother, because family and church are who you turn to here, not a government office. If it came to the worst, I'd ask Mum if we could move into the farmhouse and rent our place out to cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like standing on a roof when the wind takes the ladder. There's nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Erik that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing, at first. We'd sit at the kitchen table and look at the bills. Erik doesn't talk much when he's worried, he goes out to the shed. I'd go after him eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not a government office. Even if the help was there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if I had to, for the children, I'm not proud enough to let them go hungry. But I'd hate every minute. My father never took a penny from anyone, and I'd feel I'd let him down.

S2.say: It's wrong, and the people who built it never held a hammer in their lives or thought about towns like ours. I'd say it loud at the builders' merchant.
S2.think: I'd be terrified, because my husband and I both work at Lund's, and a robot that does roofs and walls means he needs neither of us. We have about two months saved and I won't become a computer person in two years.
S2.do: Cuts riding lessons, the football trip and the car replacement straight away. Turns to the pastor and her mother, and plans to move into her mother's farmhouse and rent out the house if things get worse.
S2.feel: Overwhelmed and trapped, with nowhere to go.
S2.quote: Like standing on a roof when the wind takes the ladder.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario hits a single point of failure: both incomes come from one small firm, savings are thin within the moderate band, and she rules out retraining. She would accept state help only for her children and feels it would betray her father. Her support system is family and church first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for the government to protect ordinary trades, if it wanted to. I'd want limits on these companies, they shouldn't be allowed to put whole towns out of work. I'd say that at the polling station, so to speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, but I still can't see what I'd become. I'm a roofer. I'd want the money as solid as we could make it before it lands, that's what I can control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, two hundred a month even if it hurts, and cut the extras. I'd talk to Lund about whether there's any part of the firm that keeps people, like repairs on old buildings. I'd vote for whoever promises to protect local trades from the big tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Five years goes by quick when your kids are growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Anna and Peter in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna's clever, she likes animals. I'd want her to be a vet, something where people need a person. Peter's ten, I'd want him to learn a trade like I did, but I'd worry it wouldn't be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't want to retrain, but five years is a long time. Is there anything you'd learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe how to use the computer for the books, so I could help Lund keep going. But not to replace myself. I'm not going to train the machine that takes my job.

S3.say: Five years is long enough for the government to protect ordinary trades if it wanted to. These companies shouldn't be allowed to put whole towns out of work.
S3.think: Five years is better, but I still can't see what I'd become, because I'm a roofer. Making the money as solid as possible before it lands is what I can control.
S3.do: Saves about 200 a month and cuts extras. Asks Lund about keeping people on repairs to old buildings, and votes for candidates who promise to protect local trades from big tech firms.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, because five years passes quickly with children growing.
S3.quote: I'm not going to train the machine that takes my job.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time gives her room to save but not to imagine a new career. Her politics turn protective: limits on big companies, not handouts. She hopes heritage repair work might stay human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for the country to get its head straight. Keep the apprenticeships, keep local firms going. I'd say it at church and to anyone at the merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I'd be fifty-three. The mortgage would be close to done and the kids mostly grown. It's still frightening, but it's a slower kind of frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Lund's, pay down the mortgage faster, and put a bit aside every month. I'd push Anna towards a job with people, like vet or nurse, and I'd keep Peter learning his trade but tell him to have a second string. I'd not retrain myself, I'd ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be with me every day, but I could carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ride it out, even if that means losing work at fifty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it comes to that, I'd do whatever honest work there is, cleaning, stacking, anything. I'm not proud about the kind of work. I'm proud about working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to do with that time, while you still can?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teach Peter properly, like my dad taught me. Even if he never uses it, I want him to know how to put a roof over his own head. That counts for something, robots or no robots.

S4.say: Ten years is time for the country to get its head straight, keep apprenticeships and keep local firms going. I'd say it at church and at the merchant.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three, with the mortgage close to done and the kids mostly grown. It's still frightening, but a slower kind of frightening.
S4.do: Keeps working at Lund's, pays down the mortgage faster and saves a little each month. Steers her daughter towards work with people and keeps teaching her son the trade with a second option in mind.
S4.feel: Anxious every day, but able to carry it.
S4.quote: I'm not proud about the kind of work. I'm proud about working.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years softens her fear but doesn't change her refusal to retrain. Her plan is to ride it out and take any honest work. Teaching her son the trade matters to her regardless of whether it pays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Erik and I both go, the town goes, and there's no time for anything. What would help is keeping local firms alive, maybe the government paying firms to keep apprentices and skilled people on, rather than paying people to stay home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If Lund's goes, and the farmers go, the whole place goes. The school, the shop, the chapel. That's what I'd really lose.

headlineQuote: If Lund's goes, and the farmers go, the whole place goes.
portrait: Rosa Jensen is a 43-year-old roofing and carpentry crew leader at a small family builder in a market town, married to a bricklayer at the same firm, with two children and about two months saved. She learned the trade from her father, never uses AI, and trusts family, church and local loyalty more than government. She's calm under a plateau and steady change, but the two-year AGI picture leaves her panicked because both household incomes depend on one small firm. With five or ten years she'd save and vote to protect local trades, refuse to retrain, and ride it out doing any honest work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband would both lose work, the town would suffer, and there'd be no time.
whatWouldHelp: Government support that pays local firms to keep apprentices and skilled workers on, rather than paying people to stay home.
